title: Why leaves turn yellow
content:
Where the yellowing starts tells you the most.
- **Older, lower leaves yellow first, evenly:** usually nitrogen deficiency. Side-dress with a nitrogen fertilizer or compost and water in.
- **Yellow between veins on older leaves:** magnesium deficiency. Apply Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate) as a foliar spray (about 20 g per litre) or a magnesium-containing fertilizer.
- **Yellow between veins on new leaves:** iron or manganese deficiency, often from high soil pH. Test pH; use chelated iron and acidify gradually if pH is above 7.5.
- **Yellowing with wilting and wet soil:** overwatering or poor drainage starving roots of oxygen. Let soil dry slightly between waterings and improve drainage.
- **Yellow leaves with brown spots or rings:** a disease such as early blight or septoria leaf spot (see leaf spot guide).
- **One side of the plant yellowing and wilting:** possible fusarium or verticillium wilt — cut a stem; brown streaks inside confirm it.
Natural ageing of a few bottom leaves on a healthy plant is normal.

title: Spots on leaves
content:
Most leaf spots are fungal or bacterial and spread in warm, wet conditions.
- **Brown spots with concentric rings and a yellow halo, starting on lower leaves:** early blight (Alternaria).
- **Small round spots with grey centres and dark edges:** septoria leaf spot.
- **Large greasy, grey-green patches that spread fast, white growth underneath in humid weather:** late blight — act immediately.
- **Small dark water-soaked spots, sometimes with yellow halos, on leaves and fruit:** bacterial spot.
- **Orange-brown powdery pustules:** rust.
**What to do:** remove and destroy (do not compost) badly affected leaves; water at the base in the morning; mulch to stop soil splashing onto leaves; space and prune for airflow; rotate crops for 2–3 years. For fungal diseases, protectant fungicides (e.g., copper, mancozeb or chlorothalonil products) slow the spread — use only products registered for your crop in your country, follow the label and observe the pre-harvest interval. Copper products also help suppress bacterial spot.

title: Tomato early and late blight
content:
**Early blight** (Alternaria solani): dark brown spots with target-like rings on older leaves, which yellow and drop. Spreads slowly from the bottom up.
**Late blight** (Phytophthora infestans): water-soaked grey-green lesions that turn brown, white fuzzy growth under leaves in humid weather, brown greasy patches on fruit. Can destroy a crop within days in cool, wet weather.
**Treatment:** 1) Remove infected leaves and badly infected plants (bag them). 2) Stop overhead watering; water at the base early in the day. 3) Prune lower leaves to 30 cm above the soil and stake plants for airflow. 4) Apply a registered protectant fungicide (copper, mancozeb or chlorothalonil) every 7–10 days in wet weather, following the label. For late blight, systemic products may be needed — ask your local extension officer or agro-dealer.
**Prevention:** resistant varieties, 3-year rotation away from tomato/potato/pepper/eggplant, mulch, and removing volunteer potato and tomato plants.

title: Blossom-end rot
content: A sunken, leathery, dark patch at the bottom of tomato or pepper fruit. It is caused by calcium not reaching the developing fruit, usually because of uneven watering rather than a lack of calcium in the soil. Keep soil evenly moist (mulch helps), avoid excess nitrogen and ammonium fertilizers, and keep soil pH around 6.2–6.8 (lime if acidic). A calcium nitrate or calcium chloride spray can help new fruit; affected fruit will not recover — remove it.

title: How often to water
content: Water deeply and less often rather than a little every day — deep watering grows deep roots. Most vegetable crops need about 25–50 mm (1–2 in) of water per week from rain plus irrigation. **Finger test:** push a finger 5 cm into the soil; water if it is dry at that depth. Water in the early morning at the base of plants. Sandy soils need water more often in smaller amounts; clay soils less often. Mulch (5–8 cm of straw or grass) reduces evaporation by a large margin. Signs of underwatering: wilting in the morning, dry crispy leaf edges. Signs of overwatering: yellow lower leaves, wilting in wet soil, root rot, fungus gnats.

title: Is my crop ready to harvest?
content:
Check days since planting against the variety's maturity days, then confirm with crop-specific signs:
- **Tomato:** first blush of colour (breaker stage) onward; full colour, slight give when ripe. Pick at breaker for distant markets — fruit ripens in transit.
- **Maize:** green mealies when silks are brown and kernels squirt milky juice; grain when the black layer forms.
- **Pepper:** full size and firm; full colour for red/yellow types.
- **Potato:** after vines die back and skins have set.
- **Cabbage:** firm, solid heads.
- **Beans:** pods snap cleanly, seeds still small.
Harvest in the cool of the morning, handle gently, keep produce in the shade and grade by size and quality before selling — graded produce fetches better prices.

title: Improving crop production
content:
The biggest gains usually come from:
1. **Soil testing** — fertilize to what the soil actually needs; correct pH with lime (most crops prefer pH 6.0–7.0).
2. **Good seed** — certified, adapted, disease-resistant varieties.
3. **Correct spacing and timely planting** — avoid overcrowding; plant at the start of reliable rains.
4. **Organic matter** — compost and manure improve water-holding and nutrients.
5. **Water management** — mulch, drip irrigation, and never stressing crops at flowering.
6. **Timely weeding** — especially the first 4–6 weeks.
7. **Integrated pest management** — scout weekly, act early, use chemicals only when needed.
8. **Crop rotation and intercropping** — e.g., legumes before maize add nitrogen and break disease cycles.
9. **Records** — track inputs, yields and prices to see what pays.

title: Nutrient deficiency signs
content:
- **Nitrogen (N):** pale green to yellow older leaves, slow growth.
- **Phosphorus (P):** dark green or purplish leaves (especially undersides), stunted plants, poor roots — common in cold soils.
- **Potassium (K):** yellow then brown scorched edges on older leaves, weak stems, poor fruit quality.
- **Magnesium (Mg):** yellow between veins of older leaves while veins stay green.
- **Calcium (Ca):** blossom-end rot, tip burn on new leaves.
- **Iron (Fe):** yellow between veins of the youngest leaves.
NPK numbers on a bag (e.g., 10-10-10) are the percentages of N, P₂O₅ and K₂O. Use a soil test to choose the product and rate.

title: Fall armyworm in maize
content: Ragged holes and 'window-pane' feeding on leaves, sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the whorl. Larvae have an inverted 'Y' on the head and four dots in a square near the tail. **Scout** 20 plants in several spots twice a week from emergence. **Act** when more than about 20% of young plants show fresh damage. Options: hand-pick larvae, apply sand/ash into the whorl on small plots, biopesticides (Bt, Metarhizium), or a registered insecticide targeted into the whorl early morning or evening. Encourage natural enemies; intercropping with legumes and push-pull systems reduce damage.

title: Common maize leaf diseases
content:
- **Grey leaf spot:** long, narrow, rectangular grey-tan lesions bounded by leaf veins.
- **Northern corn leaf blight:** long cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions (2.5–15 cm).
- **Common rust:** small cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces.
- **Maize streak virus:** fine broken yellow streaks along veins; spread by leafhoppers.
Management: resistant hybrids (the most effective step), rotation, burying or removing crop residue, balanced fertility, and registered fungicides at early disease for high-value crops. For streak virus, plant early and control grassy weeds that host leafhoppers.

title: Cabbage pests and black rot
content: **Diamondback moth:** small green caterpillars that wriggle when touched, leaving holes and 'windows'. Use Bt sprays, rotate insecticide groups to avoid resistance. **Aphids:** grey waxy clusters — spray with soapy water or a registered aphicide; conserve ladybirds. **Black rot:** V-shaped yellow lesions from leaf edges with blackened veins — use clean seed, rotate 3 years away from brassicas, remove infected plants.

title: Potato hilling and blight
content: Hill soil up around stems when plants are 15–20 cm tall and again 2–3 weeks later; this protects tubers from light (green tubers are toxic) and from tuber moth. Potatoes share early and late blight with tomatoes — scout leaves after rainy spells and protect with registered fungicides when blight is forecast. Common scab (corky patches on skins) is worse in dry, alkaline soils; keep soil moist during tuber initiation.

title: Safe pest and disease control (IPM)
content: Integrated Pest Management means: prevent first (healthy soil, resistant varieties, rotation, clean seed), scout weekly, identify correctly, and act only when damage justifies it. Start with physical and biological options (hand-picking, traps, neem-based or Bt products), then registered chemicals. When spraying: wear gloves, mask and long sleeves; never exceed the label rate; respect the pre-harvest interval; never spray during flowering when bees are active; store chemicals locked away from children and food.

title: Soil health and pH
content: Most vegetables and grains do best at pH 6.0–7.0. Acidic soils (below 5.5) lock up phosphorus and can cause aluminium toxicity — apply agricultural or dolomitic lime according to a soil test, ideally 2–3 months before planting. Add 2–5 kg of compost or well-rotted manure per square metre each season. Avoid working wet soil, keep the soil covered with mulch or cover crops, and rotate crop families.
